title: Emotion and memory can't be safely separated
subtitle: A new PTSD treatment has worrying implications
author: Dominc Wilkinson
introduction: Continuing the IAI’s current series on memory, ethicist and medical doctor Dominic Wilkinson critiques a fashionable new medical treatment, “memory reconsolidation,” which combines drugs with therapy to numb the emotional threads in painful memories. Since memory and emotion are fundamentally intertwined, Professor Wilkinson warns that this treatment could also edit the memories themselves, radically reshaping our identity. We must, he argues, place limits on the medicalization of our attempts to come to terms with emotional trauma.
body:
In my work as a specialist in newborn intensive care, I sometimes care for couples who have experienced one of the most distressing of life events—the loss of their loved newborn infant. The pain that they describe to me is all-consuming. Faced with such intense suffering, I often wish that I had something, anything, to assuage their loss. If only I had a treatment that would relieve the burden of their grief…

All of us carry happy and less happy memories. The mix of positive and negative recollections is a natural part of human existence. But for some, their memory is dominated by deeply traumatic events that have prolonged damaging effects on their ongoing lives, for example, in the form of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Others are haunted by experiences of infidelity and relationship break-up, or agonized by pain arising from loss and bereavement.

There have long been forms of talking therapy offered for painful memories. In the twentieth century, pharmacotherapy has been used for some of the symptoms arising from these (for example depression, sleeplessness and anxiety). But more recently still, there have been attempts to directly target the source. It appears that our memory may be malleable. So-called “memory reconsolidation” therapy involves the use of drugs like the medicine propranolol (long used for high blood pressure and migraine) to remove the emotional pain associated with traumatic memory. Patients with PTSD take the medicine one hour before a session that involves deliberately recalling their episode of trauma. In some studies, this appears to be effective in reducing symptoms of post-traumatic stress. Recent papers suggest that the same treatment can be effective for adjustment disorder (excessive emotional or behavioural response) after romantic betrayal. One of the treated patients described the pain of her husband’s infidelity as akin to a monster clawing out her heart. This pain persisted more than a year after she discovered his betrayal. But after three sessions of the therapy, that pain had faded into the background and she was able to get on with her life.

It appears that our memory may be malleable.

One important question is whether memory reconsolidation therapy works (the evidence is somewhat mixed). But here I will focus on a different question. If it were successful, would it be desirable to attempt to help people by numbing or even removing their memories of painful experience? Memory reconsolidation doesn’t actually erase memory, but the science of memory editing is developing rapidly, and this might be possible in the future. The 2004 film Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind famously dramatized this question. In the film, the main characters submit to a therapy that allows them to deliberately forget each other after a painful break-up. How should we think about the fictional treatment offered by the company Lacuna in Eternal Sunshine or the real memory reconsolidation treatment? Here are some reasons to be cautious.

Medicalizing

One reason relates to a concern about the marketing of maladies that are part of normal human experience. The worry is that ordinary experiences or phenomena (for example, expressions of sadness or anxiety) are pathologized in order to create a market for treatment (often of dubious efficacy). This is a real concern and potentially applies to a wide range of contemporary physical and psychological diagnoses. But we should not underestimate the significance of emotional pain for people’s lives. Some memories can be profoundly damaging, and we would have no qualms about treating acute or chronic physical pain as potent and distressing as that experienced, for example, by patients with PTSD. There is a spectrum of possible cases of memory therapy, from highly desirable forms of memory blunting to cases where this is much more questionable.

Learning

A second concern is that memories, perhaps especially negative ones, are instrumentally important for self-development. We need memories to learn; in their absence (and possibly even if they are merely emotionally neutered) we may be doomed to repeat our mistakes. In Eternal Sunshine, the central characters end up together again at the end of the film, though whether this time will be any more successful remains unclear.

However, some memories do not lead to growth and development—only to pain. There is no learning to be had from some deeply traumatic memories. Furthermore, even if there is growth to be had, sometimes that may be outweighed by the distress they cause. One practical challenge would be how patients (or professionals) can determine in advance which memories will be positive overall, even if they are painful. That may be particularly challenging if memory modification were attempted soon after a traumatic experience, as opposed to being applied for those with persistent painful memories.

Threat to the self

A deeper concern is that our memories are a fundamental part of who we are. According to some philosophers, if we were to erase them or change them in some way we would become someone different. For example, the seventeenth-century philosopher John Locke argued that the essence of a person was the conscious mind, aware of itself as persisting over time. Our thoughts and memories, and the connections between these, make us who we are. If those thoughts were magically moved into another body (Locke imagined the mind of a cobbler and a prince being swapped), our essence would go with them. He asked us to imagine, “Suppose I wholly lose the memory of some parts of my life … so that perhaps I shall not be conscious of them again … Am I … the same person that did those actions?” Locke argued that even if it was the same “man” who acted previously (carrying the same name, inhabiting the same body), this would be a distinct person or self.

So, the first thing to say is that this concern is legitimate—memories are a key part of the self. If we were to erase all of our memories, that would certainly threaten personhood (it is partly for that reason that dementia is so feared). Erasure of key parts of our memory might alter who we are to an important degree.

We are not mere computers neutrally recording the information of our senses.

Importantly, current forms of memory reconsolidation do not actually remove the painful memory—rather, they attenuate the intense and excessive emotional response to remembering. Those who had undergone treatment after being betrayed by their partner still apparently recalled what had happened. But, like a scar that has faded and contracted, the memory was no longer acutely tender, nor did it dominate their consciousness in the way it previously had. Does this mean the therapy is OK?

One view about identity and memory-based therapies is that altering the emotional value—but not the content—of our recollections is not necessarily a problem. After all, through the passage of time, or sometimes through talking therapies, we commonly come to adjust our emotional responses to past events over time. Something that was previously very painful may become much less so. That isn’t normally seen as a threat to the self

A different view is that deliberately changing the emotional valence of our memories does change the fundamental nature of those memories. After all, a key part of human experience is the value and meaning of the things that we encounter. We are not mere computers neutrally recording the information of our senses. Think, for example, of a treasured and significant memory in your past (perhaps a first love, or the birth of a child, or a significant personal achievement). Now imagine that this memory were stripped of its emotional significance to you. This memory would be more like something that happened to someone else. Our connection to that event would be very different. Perhaps if this change were permanent, we would be someone different.

The same philosophical understanding of self that points to the importance of memory also emphasizes that there is not a fixed unchanging self.

But there is a third response, inspired by Locke and some of the Western philosophers who have come after him, as well as connected to some Buddhist teachings. The same philosophical understanding of self that points to the importance of memory also emphasizes that there is not a fixed unchanging self. Who we are is influenced to a very important degree by the things that happen to us. So, for example, those who experience severe trauma or bereavement often reflect that they are not the same person as they were before these tragic events. If our self is not fixed, then the fact that therapies might change us is less striking. Change is inevitable. The important question is whether the changes to self that such therapy might bring are desired,whether they are good changes.

When we reframe the question in this way, it becomes clearer how some forms of memory modification might be positive and others negative. Where painful memories are associated with persistent damaging effects on someone’s ability to live their life, numbing or even removing those painful memories could represent a vital and positive overall change to a person.

SUGGESTED READING Memory is not stored in the brain By Victoria Trumbull

In other cases (and here bereavement is particularly salient), the memories are potentially important in and of themselves. They may be partly constitutive of someone’s “practical identity.” This idea, often linked to the American philosopher Christine Korsgaard, refers to how individuals view and define themselves—to the roles, commitments and characteristics that give them reasons to act. As painful and awful as it is for parents to cope with the loss of their child, removing the memory might be worse. I am not sure that any of the grieving parents I meet would choose to erase the memory of their infant, and many might balk at deliberately numbing that pain.

It wouldn’t be wrong to anaesthetize some painful memories, and it might even be a good thing to erase them. But memories are a key part of who we are, and who we take ourselves to be. When it comes to our minds, “spotlessness” might not be a good thing in the end.
